orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, telling her story to Lockwood, who breaks in briefly at the start. Nelly says these events happened 'last winter', so the chapter covers the winter, spring and early summer of 1801. Edgar Linton has just put a stop to Cathy's secret visits to her cousin Linton at Wuthering Heights.

notes.t: amusing a stranger to the family
notes.g: Entertaining someone from outside the family.
notes.n: 'Amuse' could simply mean keep someone interested or occupied.
Nelly is teasing Lockwood: she thinks he is falling for the young widow he met at Wuthering Heights.

notes.t: hang her picture over your fireplace
notes.g: Lockwood has asked for a picture of 'her' in his sitting room.
notes.n: Nelly takes this as a sign that he is more interested in young Catherine than he admits.

notes.g: Putting myself in the way of temptation.
I belong to the busy world of towns and society.
notes.n: Lockwood reminds Nelly (and us) that he is only a visitor to these moors.
The word is usually used for leaving property in a will. Edgar's advice is the one thing he can be sure of leaving her.

notes.g: Nelly's proper first name; Edgar always uses it.
Linton Heathcliff, son of Edgar's sister Isabella and Heathcliff.

notes.m: Not 'dainty' or 'refined'. 'Delicate' here means in poor health.

notes.g: Not likely to live to be a grown man.
Too strong-willed for her to manage.
Far too soft and giving with him.

notes.t: it wants four years and more to his being of age
notes.g: It will be over four years before he is 21, legally an adult.
notes.n: Linton is about sixteen. Until 21 a young person was a minor in law: they could not control their own property, and needed a parent's or guardian's consent to marry.
'Kirk' is the northern English and Scottish word for church. Cathy's mother is buried in its churchyard (Chapter XVI).

notes.g: Evergreen conifer trees, often planted in churchyards.

notes.n: A soliloquy is a speech a character makes alone, as in a play.

notes.t: the approach of what is coming
notes.n: Edgar has long looked forward to dying, so that he can lie beside his wife.

notes.g: That narrow valley (leading up to the church).
A man on his wedding day.
notes.n: Edgar married Catherine at this church.

notes.g: Buried in that quiet churchyard in the hollow.

notes.t: the green mound of her mother’s grave
notes.n: Catherine was buried in a corner of the churchyard near the moor, not in the Linton family chapel (Chapter XVI). Edgar wants to lie beside her there.

notes.m: Not 'stop doing'. To 'quit' a person or place meant to leave them.

notes.g: Here 'Linton' is young Linton Heathcliff, Edgar's nephew.
notes.n: Linton is his first name; it was his mother's maiden name.

notes.g: Comfort her when I am dead.

notes.t: a feeble tool to his father
notes.g: A weak instrument his father uses for his own purposes.
Keep on, even though it is hard.

notes.n: Edgar means he would rather she died before him than be left to Heathcliff. Nelly answers with the other sense of the phrase: trust her to God's care now.

notes.g: In God's care and according to God's plan.
notes.n: 'Providence' is God's guiding care for the world.

notes.g: Inexperienced ideas; her young way of seeing things.

notes.t: his cheek was often flushed, and his eyes were bright
notes.g: Signs of fever, which Cathy mistakes for health.
notes.n: Flushed cheeks and glittering eyes were well-known signs of wasting illnesses such as consumption (tuberculosis).

notes.g: Cathy's birthday was also the day her mother died.
notes.n: Edgar always spent it alone and walked to the grave at dusk (Chapter XXI). So March 1801.

notes.g: If the sick boy had been fit to be seen.
Being told what to write (by Heathcliff).

notes.n: Nelly's dry hint: the polished part of the letter that follows was Heathcliff's work, not Linton's.

notes.m: Not a job interview or a press interview.

notes.g: Make me not good enough for.

notes.m: 'Society' here means company, not the community or high society.
Nothing to do with being engaged to be married.

notes.n: A grand, rather biblical word, as in the Epistles of St Paul.
From playing the same string of a harp over and over.

notes.g: A strong supporter on his side.
With me as her chaperone and protector.

notes.t: set aside yearly a portion of his income for my young lady’s fortune
notes.g: Saved part of his income each year as money for Cathy.
notes.n: A woman's 'fortune' was the money she brought to a marriage or lived on. Edgar has to save it up because the Grange estate itself will not go to her (see the next notes).

notes.g: Thrushcross Grange, the Linton family home.
A marriage to the person who will inherit his estate: Linton.
notes.n: Under old Mr. Linton's arrangements, if Edgar had no son the estate passed to Isabella's line, not to Edgar's daughter (Chapters X and XVI). Settlements like this, called entails, kept land in the male line. So marrying Linton is the only way Cathy can keep her home.
'Master' was the polite title for a boy or young man. His surname is Heathcliff.

notes.g: My fears that something bad was coming.
Force him to seem so keen.
